position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, emphasizing status, convenience, and brand prestige, while leveraging the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment, such as market demand, technical feasibility, or competitive advantage.
Consider the existing B2B2C model of independent dealer distribution and the current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming, or homeowner tasks) using tractor engineering.
2) Expand the existing B2B2C model by deepening dealer relationships and offering additional service or parts to individual buyers without a new differentiated proposition.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on the current B2B2C model of farm and industrial equipment sold through independent dealers.
4) Target a different customer group (e.g., small‑farm owners, urban gardeners, or DIY enthusiasts) with a proposition tailored to their needs, using the same tractor platform.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: In 1962, the market was small but growing; homeowners perceived tractors as a status signal and a way to modernize their outdoor space, leading them to purchase even if the market was limited.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can charge premium prices for a differentiated model, sell through independent dealers who can offer financing and service, and build brand loyalty that supports future product lines.

X1.name: Consumer Proposition Pilot Test
X1.method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: Condition A sees a status‑focused lawn tractor description emphasizing prestige, convenience, and brand prestige; Condition B sees a reliability‑focused description emphasizing ease of use, durability, and trust from farm equipment. Both conditions present the same product details (e.g., 110 model, basic attachments). Participants indicate whether they would purchase at a price point of $2,500 and provide a reason. Data are analyzed to compare purchase intent and reason across conditions.
X1.sample: 300 homeowners aged 25–65 with household income over $50,000, recruited via an online panel. Randomly assign 150 to Condition A and 150 to Condition B.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and primary reason for purchase (open‑ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher purchase intent and status/reason in Condition A (status‑focused).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher purchase intent and reliability/ease‑of‑use reason in Condition B (reliability‑focused).

X1.decision_rule: If Condition A’s purchase intent exceeds Condition B’s by at least 10 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), proceed with the differentiated consumer proposition (support T1). If Condition B’s intent exceeds Condition A’s by at least 10 percentage points and the difference is statistically significant, develop a reliability‑focused proposition (support T2). If neither difference meets the threshold, maintain the current B2B2C model.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for homeowners, emphasizing status, convenience, and brand prestige, while leveraging the existing dealer network to reach individual buyers.
final.target_customer: Homeowners aged 25–65 with household income over $50,000 who need a reliable, easy‑to‑use tool for small‑scale landscaping and gardening.
final.value_proposition: A premium‑priced lawn tractor that combines Deere’s engineering reputation with status and convenience, sold through independent dealers offering financing and service, creating higher‑margin sales and brand extension.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Proposition Pilot Test (300 homeowners, 10‑week survey) to measure purchase intent and reason under status‑focused versus reliability‑focused messaging.
final.uncertainty: The actual demand for a differentiated consumer proposition in 1962 is unknown; the test will resolve whether homeowners are willing to pay a premium for status and convenience.
would_change_if: If the pilot shows purchase intent for the status‑focused condition is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the reliability‑focused condition and the difference is statistically significant (p < 0.05), we would proceed with the T1‑
If neither condition meets the threshold, we would maintain the current B2B2C model.

Offer a differentiated consumer proposition (e.g., a compact lawn tractor) at a premium price (e.g., $1,200) and provide financing options. Track sales over 12 weeks and collect post-purchase surveys on motivation (status vs. reliability/ease of use).
X1.sample: 10 homes in the target area (e.g., suburban Johnson County, Iowa, where Deere has a strong dealer network).
X1.measure: Number of units sold and average price paid; survey responses on primary purchase motivation.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Sales will exceed 5 units per week, and at least 60% of respondents will cite reliability/ease of use as the primary reason for purchase.

Participants are randomly assigned to view either a description of a Deere lawn tractor positioned as a single‑tool solution for light landscaping (T1) or the same description re‑framed as a versatile tool that reduces the need for multiple hand tools and rental equipment (T2). X1.sample: 500 homeowners recruited from a panel in the United States, balanced across age, income, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: maximum price participants would pay for the lawn tractor. Secondary outcomes: binary purchase intent (would buy) and willingness to pay above standard garden tools.

arguments.name: Homeowner Preference Test: Lawn Tractor vs. Manual Tools
arguments.method: Online survey with a randomized between‑subjects design. Participants are randomly assigned to view either a description of a Deere lawn tractor positioned as a single‑tool solution for light landscaping (T1) or the same description re‑framed as a versatile tool that reduces the need for multiple hand tools and rental equipment (T2). They are then asked to indicate their willingness to purchase the product at a price above standard garden tools and to state the maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 homeowners recruited from a panel in the United States, balanced across age, income, and geographic region to ensure representativeness.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: maximum price participants would pay for the lawn tractor. Secondary outcomes: binary purchase intent (would buy) and willingness to pay above standard garden tools.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants assigned to the lawn tractor description will report a higher maximum price and higher purchase intent than those assigned to the versatile‑tool description.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants assigned to the versatile‑tool description will report a higher maximum price and higher purchase intent than those assigned to the lawn tractor description.

arguments.decision_rule: If the mean maximum price reported by the lawn tractor group exceeds the mean maximum price reported by the versatile‑tool group by at least €50 (a threshold of €50), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for light landscaping. If the difference is less than €50, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for small-scale landscaping and hobby farming, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. The evidence shows a prototype was built in 1959 and production began in 1963, indicating technical feasibility. The 76‑percent rise in lawn and garden equipment sales in the 1960s suggests market demand, and the existing B2B2C model with independent dealers provides a viable channel.
